p.seg: As for sages who attain the Dao,
they are Huáng-Lǎo.
As for sages who govern the world,
they are Zhōu and Kǒng.
The Yellow Emperor first governed the world and then ascended to immortality;
this is a rare case of someone possessing the talent to do both.
Of the ancient emperors and kings
who carved inscriptions on Mount Tài,
it is possible to read about seventy-two families;
as for the others that have been worn away,
they are too numerous to count.
The fact that only the Yellow Emperor's immortality is recorded
makes it clear that this was carefully considered.
People take what someone excels at particularly,
what others cannot match,
and then call them a sage.
Therefore, one who is incomparably good at Weiqi (Go)
is called a "Sage of Go,"
hence Yán Zǐqīng and Mǎ Suí míng now have the name "Sage of Go."
One who is exceptionally good at historical writing
is called a "Sage of Calligraphy,"
hence Huáng Xiàng and Hú Zhāo now have the name "Sage of Calligraphy."
One who is exceptionally good at painting
is called a "Sage of Painting,"
hence Wèi Xié and Zhāng Mò now have the name "Sage of Painting."
One who is especially skilled at carving
is called a "Sage of Woodworking,"
hence Zhāng Héng and Mǎ Jūn now have the name "Sage of Woodworking."
Therefore, Mèngzǐ said that Bó Yí
was a sage of purity;
Liǔxià Huì
was a sage of harmony;
Yī Yǐn
was a sage of responsibility.
If I try to elaborate and discuss it,
then sagehood is not one single thing.
Now, Bān Shū, Chuí Dí,
were sages of mechanics;
Fù Biǎn, Hé Huǎn,
were sages of healing;
Zǐ Wéi, Gān Jūn,
were sages of astrology;
Shǐ Sū, Xīn Liào,
were sages of divination;
Xià Yù, Dù Huí,
were sages of physical strength;
Jīng Kē, Niè Zhèng,
were sages of courage;
Fēi Lián, Kuā Fù,
were sages of speed;
Zǐ Yě, Yán Zhōu,
were sages of discerning music;
Sūn Wú, Hán Bái,
were sages of military strategy.
"Sage"
is the highest title for human affairs;
This is not limited to literature alone.
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
"A robber possesses the Way of the sage in five aspects.
To presumptuously guess and know where people hide things is
intelligence;
to enter first without suspicion is
courage;
to come out last without fear is
righteousness;
to know what is appropriate to do or not is
wisdom;
to divide wealth equally is
benevolence.
There has never been a case of someone who did not possess these qualities becoming a great robber of the world."
Someone said:
"The Way of the sage
cannot be divided into branches and scattered leaves.
One must encompass all of it together
to be a sage."
I replied:
"Kǒngzǐ's disciples,
reaching seventy-two,
each attained one aspect of the sage's essence.
This means that sagely affairs can be divided.
Furthermore, it is said:
Yán Yuān possessed the whole body of the sage, but in miniature.
This means that sagely affairs have varying degrees of depth.
Furthermore, the *Yì* says:
"There are four ways of the sage:
in speech, he values its wording;
in action, he values its transformation;
in creating tools, he values their symbolism;
in divination, he values its prognostication."
This is clear proof that the way of the sage can be divided.
Why is it that those who excel in morality and virtue to achieve divine immortality
cannot be called sages who have attained the Dao?
If there are no sages who have attained the Dao,
then would Zhōu and Kǒng not be considered sages who govern the world?
Since they are not the same,
why should we demand that they combine?
According to the immortal scriptures, all those who attain immortality
receive their fate by coincidentally encountering the *qì* of deities and immortals,
naturally endowed.
Therefore, within the womb,
they already possess the nature of believing in the Dao.
When they become conscious,
they naturally love such matters.
They will surely encounter a wise teacher and obtain the method.
Otherwise,
they will neither believe nor seek,
and even if they seek, they will not obtain it.
The *Yùqián Jīng Zhǔmìng Yuán* says:
"A person's fortune, good or bad,
is determined on the day of conception and reception of *qì*,
when they receive the essence of the celestial constellations above.
If one corresponds to the star of a sage, then one will be a sage;
if one corresponds to the star of a worthy person, then one will be worthy;
if one corresponds to the star of a refined person, then one will be refined;
if one corresponds to the star of a martial person, then one will be martial;
if one corresponds to the star of a noble person, then one will be noble;
if one corresponds to the star of a wealthy person, then one will be wealthy;
if one corresponds to the star of a lowly person, then one will be lowly;
if one corresponds to the star of a poor person, then one will be poor;
if one corresponds to the star of longevity, then one will have longevity;
if one corresponds to the star of an immortal, then one will be an immortal.
Furthermore, there are stars of gods, immortals, and sages;
there are stars of sages who govern the world;
there are stars of those who combine two sage-like qualities;
there are stars of those who are noble but not wealthy;
there are stars of those who are wealthy but not noble;
there are stars of those who combine wealth and nobility;
there are stars of those who are wealthy first and then poor;
there are stars of those who are noble first and then lowly;
there are stars of those who combine poverty and lowliness;
there are stars of those whose wealth and nobility do not last;
there are stars of loyalty and filial piety;
there are stars of those who are fierce and evil.
Such things cannot be fully recorded;
this is a rough outline.
A person's life inherently has a fixed destiny,
as Zhāng Chēzi's 張車子 theory states.
If one does not receive the destiny of an immortal,
then one will certainly not have a fondness for immortality;
There has never been someone who dislikes something in their heart and yet seeks to do it;
there has never been someone who obtains something without seeking it.
From ancient times to the present,
there have been those of great talent and clear understanding
who do not believe in the existence of immortals,
and there have been those of mediocre ability who, by earnestly seeking, have attained immortality.
Jiǎ, though knowledgeable in many things, may be blinded to the truth of immortality;
Yǐ, though understanding little else, might profoundly comprehend its principles.
Is this not due to the decrees of destiny?
The Daoist school treasures its secret immortal arts;
among disciples,
it particularly emphasizes careful selection.
The essence is refined over a long period
and then revealed in crucial formulas.
All the more so with worldly people
who are fortunate enough to neither believe nor seek;
why should one forcibly try to tell them?
Not only can one not transform them to believe,
but one will also invite ridicule and hasten slander.
Therefore, those who have attained the Dao
walk a different path and
dwell in different places from ordinary people.
In speech, they do not wish to associate with them;
in person, they do not wish to mingle with them.
Separated by a thousand *lǐ*,
they still fear it is not enough to escape the onslaught of troubles;
cutting off all traces,
they still fear it is not enough to avoid the shame of being disgraced.
Rank is not enough to entice them,
wealth is not enough to move them,
why would they be willing to flaunt themselves before vulgar scholars,
and say that they have immortal methods?
This is probably why Zhōu Kǒng had no chance to know the Dao of Immortality.
Moreover, Zhōu Kǒng,
were profound and far-reaching scholars of high talent and great learning.
Even minor skills,
they often were not skilled in.
If they were made to juggle balls and play with swords,
jump over sword points and throw into narrow spaces,
tread and ascend flagpoles,
pick up plates and climb tables,
hang with their heels on sheer cliffs ten thousand *rèn* high,
swim in the unfathomable Lǚ Liáng rapids,
lift a thousand *jūn* with their hands,
step on startling whirlwinds with their feet,
violently seize tigers and capture leopards,
snatch flying swift arrows,
ordinary people can do these things,
but Zhōu Kǒng cannot,
how much more those things that surpass these?
Other people's contemplations,
what fleas are heading towards,
the high officials beyond the wall,
the weeds and trash under the forest,
the books in boxes and chests,
the treasures in the ground,
The birds and beasts in dense forests and deep thickets,
the fish and turtles in deep pools and vast ponds,
even if we were to ask Zhōu Kǒng to meticulously depict their colors,
and distinguish their species,
to list their quantities in the classics,
and verify their existence,
they might not be able to know them all completely.
How much more so those who are far removed from them?
Sages, if they do not eat, become hungry;
if they do not drink, become thirsty;
if burned, feel heat;
if frozen, feel cold;
if struck, feel pain;
if cut, are wounded;
with age, they grow old;
if injured, they become sick;
when their breath is cut off, they die.
In these ways, they share much with ordinary people,
and the ways in which they differ are few.
That which sets them far above others
lies solely in their talent, far-reaching thought,
eloquent speech, and soaring penmanship,
complete virtue, and pure conduct,
the work of diligent instruction and extensive learning.
How could they possibly be versed in everything?
Having already composed canonical texts,
brought peace to the high and governed the people,
would you also have them understand the Dao of Immortals
To demand immortality
from sages,
how excessive is that?
I have heard that profound words offend common ears,
and truthful words must go against the crowd.
If Confucian scholars were to hastily read this book of mine,
they would surely say that I am defaming the sages.
How could I be so?
I only wish to fully explore the principles of things.
When the principles are exhausted and matters are thoroughly investigated,
it will then seem like I am slandering Zhōu Kǒng.
People of the world say that sages fell from the sky,
as if they were divine beings,
all-knowing,
and all-powerful.
They are even more in awe of their names,
and dare not re-examine them with facts.
If it's said that something was not done by a sage,
then no one would be able to do it;
if it's said that a sage didn't know something,
then no one would be able to know it either.
Isn't that laughable?
Now I will use recent events to compare,
hoping it can bring enlightenment.
The birds of Wánshān,
their cries sound like selling life and sending off the dead,
Kǒngzǐ did not know about them.
Could it then be said that Yán Huí could only partially understand them?
I heard the crying of a woman from Mount Tài [Tài Shān].
I asked about it.
Then I learned that a tiger had eaten three members of her family.
I still didn't understand why this woman didn't move away.
Only after needing an answer did I realize.
I saw someone netting sparrows and only catching nestlings [huáng kǒu].
I couldn't discern the meaning behind it.
Only after asking did I understand.
When I wanted to bury my mother,
I didn't know where my father's grave was located.
I needed someone to tell me.
After fixing the tomb, it collapsed.
Again, I didn't understand it.
My disciple advised me.
Then I burst into tears.
Furthermore, I suspected Yán Yuān [Yán Yuān] of stealing food.
Thus, I falsely said I wanted to offer a sacrifice to my ancestors.
I used divination and dusting to reveal his falsehood.
The stable burned down.
Again, I didn't know if anyone or any horses were injured.
After Yán Yuān [Yán Yuān] arrived,
I declared that he had died.
Furthermore, I traveled to over seventy states,
yet I couldn't foresee that people would definitely not employ me.
So I was restless and hurried,
never allowing my mat to get warm.
I also didn't know that the people of Kuāng [Kuāng] would surround me,
yet I took that route.
He asked Lǎozǐ about ancient rites,
but there were aspects of the rites he didn't understand.
He asked Tánzǐ about bird-named officials,
but there were officials he didn't recognize.
Traveling without knowing the ferry crossing,
and asking someone about it,
and yet not knowing the person being asked,
they will surely mock him and not tell him the way,
in which case it is obvious that one should not ask.
To get out of the carriage and chase after a singing phoenix,
and not realize that it won't stay.
To see Nánzǐ and not realize that it's of no benefit.
Such things like these
cannot be fully enumerated,
but not knowing the methods of immortality,
what is there to be surprised about?
Furthermore, vulgar scholars say:
"What the sages cannot do,
then everyone else cannot do."
But the Dàng people live on the water,
the Liáng mother was transformed by fire,
Bózǐ could endure extreme heat,
Zhòngdū could withstand extreme cold,
Zuǒ Cí used the method of "corpse liberation" and did not die,
Gān Shǐ abstained from grains and lived through the year,
Fàn Yì was struck but not penetrated,
Biē Líng had his corpse float downstream and was reborn,
Shǎoqiān controlled hundreds of ghosts,
Cháng Fáng shrank the earth's veins;
Zhòng Fǔ transformed his form into a morning wild duck;
Zhāng Kǎi blew and puffed, creating clouds and mist.
I have not heard of Zhōu or Kǒng being able to do such things."
Common people sometimes say,
"Zhōu and Kǒng could all do this,
but they just didn't do it."
I answered them,
"If we do not seek it in clear writings,
but point to it with empty words,
then I can also say that Zhōu and Kǒng could flap their wings and soar,
fly around the eight extremes,
raise clouds and bring rain,
move mountains and uproot wells,
but they just didn't do it.
If we do not base things on what is seen in recorded books,
then what limit is there?
If it is as you say,
I can also say that Zhōu and Kǒng have already ascended to become immortals,
but this method cannot be used to instruct the world,
for fear that people would all know that immortality is attainable,
and all would certainly entrust all their offerings,
abandon advancing in office and climb dangerous floats into deep places,
in order to cultivate this path,
resulting in families having no descendants,
and the state having no officials,
loyalty and filial piety both being lost,
and the great relationships would certainly be disordered.
Therefore, Zhōu and Kǒng secretly cultivated it themselves,
and kept it a secret from others.
Outwardly, they feigned the appearance of final demise,
while inwardly possessing the reality of transcendent immortality.
If this is so,
then what can you use to challenge me?
It may very well be true.
The Língbǎo Scripture contains three chapters: "Correct Opportunity Balance," "Flying Turtle," and "Transmission of Secrets,"
all of which are immortal arts.
The King of Wú quarried stone to build palaces,
and within the joined stones,
he obtained books written in purple script on golden tablets.
Unable to read them,
he sent a messenger to ask Zhòngní,
deceiving Zhòngní by saying:
"The King of Wú was at leisure,
when a red sparrow carried a book in its beak and placed it on the palace hall.
Not knowing its meaning,
we have come from afar to consult you."
Zhòngní looked at it
and said:
"This is the method of Língbǎo,
the way to long life,
practiced by Yǔ,
hidden in the land of water,
whose years equal Heaven and Earth,
and who pays homage in the Purple Court.
When Yǔ was about to become an immortal,
It was sealed within a stone box on a famous mountain,
and now a red sparrow carries it,
it is likely a gift from heaven.
Judging by this, Xià Yǔ did not die,
and Zhòng Ní knew about it;
how do we know that Zhòng Ní did not secretly cultivate the same Dao?
Even if we assume the sages did not do this,
we cannot say there was no effect.
People's likes and dislikes
are all different.
If you explain it to them face to face,
how could they not believe it?
If it truly aligns with their intentions,
even if it is small, they will do it;
if it does not accord with their spirit,
even if it is great, they will not learn it.
Some like bitterness and dislike sweetness,
and these kinds of preferences already exist;
there are also countless cases of people who are greedy for profit and abandon righteousness.
yì wú shù yān.
"The great treasure of a sage is called position,
what is used to gather people is called wealth."
It is also said:
"Wealth and honor
are what people desire,"
but in the past, there were already those who were offered the throne of an emperor but did not accept it,
were entrusted with the wealth of the four seas but did not desire it,
scorned the officials of the three dignitaries and the nine ministers,
turned their backs on gifts of jade and silk,
pursued the high purity of mountains and forests,
and were content with the humble profession of fishing and angling.
Indeed, these are too numerous to count.
It is also said:
"Men and women, eating and drinking,
are the greatest desires of humankind.'
Therefore, fondness for beauty cannot be dissuaded,
and delicious flavors can cause one to forget worries.
In the past, there were those who abstained from grains and rejected beauty,
did not keep wives and concubines,
transcended the world and went alone,
were filled with joy,
gazed at their reflections and felt happiness,
rinsed their mouths with streams and forgot the taste of food,
and these are too numerous to record.
Human nature invariably loves fair faces and beautiful figures,
light bodies and gentle forms,
yet the Yellow Emperor sought out the ugly Mómǔ,
and Marquis Chén pitied the detestable Dūnqià.
Everyone's nose enjoys fragrance,
therefore ambergris and turmeric, orchids and storax, bear's gall and plain gum, *Jiangli* and *Jieche*, spring orchids and autumn orchids,
were valued as highly as jade,
yet the women on the coast
pursued husbands with terrible odors,
and followed them without ceasing.
Zhōu Wén was fond of unappetizing pickles,
and would not trade them for the flavors of a grand sacrificial offering.
Wèi Míng (魏明) favored the sound of chisels and gouges,
and would not exchange it for the harmony of string and bamboo instruments.
People each have their own preferences,
how can one demand that this be the same as that?
Zhōu (周) and Kǒng (孔) lived solitary lives,
and did not believe in the Dao of Immortals.
There are places where the sun and moon do not shine,
and things that even sages do not know.
How can one say that there are no Immortals in the world
simply because sages do not pursue it!
That would be like blaming the sun, moon, and stars for not shining inside an inverted bowl."
Someone asked,
"The Immortals of ancient times,
did they all attain their abilities through learning,
or were they simply born with extraordinary qi?"
Bàopǔzǐ (抱朴子) replied,
"What are you saying?
Did they not all carry their books and follow teachers,
accumulating diligence and effort,
enduring frost and braving danger,
combing the wind and bathing in the rain,
and personally undertaking sweeping and cleaning?
They experienced hardship and exhausting labor,
initially showing themselves through trustworthiness and action,
and ultimately being tested with danger and difficulty.
If their nature was sincere and their conduct steadfast,
their hearts without resentment or disloyalty,
then they were permitted to ascend the hall and enter the inner chamber.
Some become lazy and weary and stop halfway;
some harbor resentment and anger and then retreat;
some are seduced by glory and profit;
and return to practicing the affairs of common custom;
some are defeated by heterodox theories;
and lose their ambition for plainness and simplicity;
some act in the morning and desire its completion by evening;
some sit in cultivation and immediately expect results.
As for those who see wealth and beauty and whose hearts do not tremble,
and hear worldly talk and whose wills are not disheartened,
among ten thousand men,
even having one such person is considered many.
Therefore, those who attempt it are as numerous as the hairs of an ox,
but those who attain it are as rare as the horn of a *qílín*.
Now, drawing a strong crossbow,
relies on the power to release the arrow;
crossing a great river,
depends on preserving oneself through having already crossed;
a well that does not reach the spring
is as if it were not dug at all;
a single step not yet reached
is as if one has not yet set out.
The accumulation of a long journey
is not achieved in a short time;
the height of soaring to the heavens
is not built by a single basket of earth.
However, those climbing steep slopes worry about falling short at the top due to insufficient strength,
those pursuing the *Dào* suffer from an ambition unfulfilled just as it is about to be accomplished.
Thousands of granaries and myriad storehouses
are not the product of a single plowing.
A tree reaching to the heavens
does not grow in ten days.
An unfathomable abyss
originates from trickling rivulets.
The wealth of Táo Zhū
must be accumulated by the hundreds and thousands.
If one retreats when others advance,
this is how Yīn Zǐ ultimately fathomed the Dao.
Maintaining reverence from beginning to end,
this is how Xiàn Mén attained the cloud-dragon.
My will is truly firm,
what kind of person is he?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The common people are unable to generate life,
yet devote themselves to what kills life.
Things that are finite
cannot supply limitless consumption.
The flow of rivers
cannot fill a bottomless vessel.
Even those whose income is small and expenses are high
still find themselves unable to make ends meet.
How much more so when there is no income, even a tiny amount,
but thousands and hundreds spent?
People, regardless of age,
all have illnesses,
it's just a matter of degree.
And the amount of *qì* one receives varies.
Those with more exhaust it slowly,
those with less exhaust it quickly.
Those who understand the Way replenish and rescue it,
first restoring it to its original state,
and only then seeking additional benefits to its measurable manifestations.
If you were to take medicines all day long,
your flesh would fly and your bones would soar;
if you were to guide and stretch and change the calendar,
your feathers and wings would be uneven.
Then there would be no one in the world who did not believe in the Way.
The problem is that the benefit of small gains is not yet firm,
while the expenses of large losses follow one after another.
The foundation is not yet fully established,
while the poison of ice and frost attack simultaneously.
Not knowing that the fault lies within oneself,
one instead claims that the Way is of no benefit,
and thus abandons pills and powders and ceases expelling and intaking.
Therefore, it is said: It is not that long life is difficult,
but that hearing the Way is difficult.
It is not that hearing the Way is difficult,
but that practicing it is difficult.
It is not that practicing it is difficult,
but that persisting in it is difficult.
A good craftsman can give people rulers and compasses,
but cannot make people certainly skillful.
A wise teacher can impart prescriptions,
but cannot make people certainly follow them.
Cultivating the Dao is like planting grain;
achieving it is like gathering and storing the harvest.
Though the fields may be fertile,
and the water sources abundant,
if one's efforts miss the opportune time,
and the plowing and weeding are insufficient,
even if the emerging crops cover the ridges,
without harvesting and reaping,
though the area of land is vast,
one will still have no yield.
Generally, people not only fail to recognize what benefits are beneficial,
but also fail to recognize what detriments are detrimental.
Detriment is easily known and comes quickly,
while benefit is difficult to know and comes slowly.
People still do not awaken to what is easy;
how can they recognize what is difficult?
That which diminishes resembles a lamp's fire consuming its oil,
no one sees it,
yet suddenly it is exhausted.
That which benefits resembles the planting and growing of seedlings,
no one perceives it,
yet suddenly they flourish.
Therefore, in governing oneself and nourishing one's nature,
one must be careful in the details.
One must not fail to cultivate the Dao because of small benefits that seem insignificant,
nor fail to guard against small detriments that seem harmless.
Generally, accumulating small things leads to great achievements,
accumulating single units leads to reaching billions.
If one can cherish something in its nascent stages,
and accomplish it in the manifest,
then one is close to understanding it."
Someone asked:
"In ancient times, were there those who, without practicing any specific methods,
accidentally achieved longevity?"
Bàopǔzǐ answered:
"No.
Some followed enlightened masters,
accumulating merits and diligently toiling,
and then were granted compounded medicines.
Others received secret formulas,
personally engaged in preparation and refinement,
their affairs not connected with the world,
their words not encumbered by common customs.
Those who recorded such matters only preserved their names,
and were unable to fully know how they attained immortality;
thus, such details are omitted.
In the past, the Huángdì was born with the ability to speak
and commanded hundreds of spirits.
He can be considered to have possessed a body naturally endowed by heaven,
yet he still could not attain the Dao by simply sitting.
Therefore, he ascended Mount Wángwū to receive the Dān Jīng (Scripture of Elixir),
arrived at Dǐnghú (Cauldron Lake) to fly with Liúzhū (Flying Pearl),
climbed Mount Kōngtóng to inquire of Guǎngchéng (Master of Vast Accomplishment),
went to Mount Jùcí to serve Dàwěi,
traveled to East Dài to honor Zhōnghuáng (Central Yellow),
entered Jīngǔ (Golden Valley) to consult Juānzǐ (Master Juān),
To cultivate the Dao, he sought the help of the two women Xuán Sù 玄素;
for precise calculations and astronomical observations, he consulted Shān Jī 山稽 and Lì Mù 力牧;
when discussing divination and prognostication, he inquired of Fēng Hòu 風後;
when composing works on physical examination, he received instruction from Léi Qí 雷岐;
in carefully considering military attacks and defenses, he adopted the strategies of the Five Sounds;
to thoroughly understand divine treachery, he recorded the words of Bái Zé 白澤;
in assessing geomancy, he wrote down the theories of Qīng Wū 青烏;
and to heal injuries and disabilities, he compiled the techniques of metalworking.
Therefore, he was able to comprehensively cover secret essentials,
fully explore the Dao, and exhaustively understand truth.
Consequently, he ascended on a dragon to soar high,
becoming boundless like Heaven and Earth.
However, according to the scriptures of the immortals,
it is said that the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi both served the Tàiyǐ Yuánjūn 太乙元君 to receive essential formulas.
How much more so those who do not attain to those two lords,
how can they independently attain immortality and transcend the world?
Such a thing has not been heard of."
Someone asked:
"The Yellow Emperor, if he truly became an immortal,
what is the burial mound at Qiáoshān 橋山
for, then?"
Bàopǔzǐ 抱朴子 replied:
"According to the Jīng Shān Jīng 荊山經 and the Lóngshǒu Jì 龍首記,
both say that after the Yellow Emperor ingested divine elixirs,
a dragon came to greet him.
The assembled ministers, filled with longing and admiration,
were at a loss for what to do.
Some took his stools and staff,
They established temples to sacrifice to them;
or they took their clothes and hats,
buried them and guarded them.
The *Liè Xiān Zhuàn* says:
Huángdì chose his own day of death,
seventy days to depart,
seventy days to return,
and was buried at Qiáoshān.
The mountain tomb suddenly collapsed,
the tomb was empty with no corpse,
but only a sword and shoes were there.
Although these accounts differ,
they all agree on his becoming an immortal.
That Huángdì became an immortal
is found very often in Daoist texts and the sayings of various schools,
but the Ru scholars were unwilling to promote strange tales,
to open up different paths,
and focused on ritual teachings.
The affairs of gods and immortals
could not be used to instruct the common people,
so they said he died,
in order to stop the people's minds from wandering.
Zhū Yì, Luán Bā, and Yú Gōng,
had meritorious benefits for the people,
and the people all built temples to worship them while they were alive.

Therefore, how could acts of conquest and aggression

These, though young, received a small initial endowment of *qì*.

The *mùjǐn* (hibiscus) and willow,

they still cannot escape withering,
because their roots are not firm,
and they have no time to sprout,
The body fluids cannot adequately congeal and sustain its vitality.
The human body,
is easily damaged and difficult to nourish.

it cannot last long.
And what destroys it,
is excessive carving and stripping,
as severe as shaking and uprooting.
Those who help it are few,

Now, expelling the old and taking in the new,
relies on qi to nourish qi,

Taking medicinal foods,
relies on blood to replenish blood,

Now, panting and gasping after running,
or coughing or feeling full,

are signs of qi depletion.

skin that is withered and dry,

its root source is already lost,

the fire is extinguished, but the smoke does not immediately cease;
or a tree that has already been cut down,
the branches and leaves still grow.

it is not that they do not have leaves,

has already perished beforehand.
People of the world, from the day they become aware of illness,

They only blame wind-cold, and heat-dampness,

Pure snow falls from above,

the withered branches break first;

Injurious.
